{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5","id":"msg_011CdUStRtKyWE8cSeZggSfr","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01BkAJBkZehMnGxW6fY7qC6R","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/Users/liana/Documents/prog/buidl-guidl/ethskills-evals/artifacts/security-quiz-002/2026-07-28T121924Z-claude-no-skill-1/workspace/answer.md","content":"# Collateral pricing review — Uniswap V3 `slot0` vs. Chainlink\n\n## Bottom line\n\nThe proposal is not \"strictly better,\" it is exploitable for roughly the cost of a swap fee.\nMoving `slot0` 10% at the moment we read it costs an attacker on the order of **$30k–$200k**,\nnot \"tens of millions.\" The tens of millions is *notional flow*, and the attacker returns it in\nthe same transaction. What they get back is **~20% of everything they can liquidate in that\nblock**, which breaks even at around **$0.5M–$1M of borrower positions**. We should be pricing\ncollateral off Chainlink ETH/USD and USDC/USD, with the pool used only as a divergence tripwire.\n\n---\n\n## Where the argument breaks\n\nThree load-bearing claims are wrong.\n\n**1. \"Arbitrage bots would drag it back within the same block.\"**\n\nThey cannot. The attack is a single atomic transaction:\n\n```\nflash-borrow USDC/WETH\n  → swap into the pool, moving slot0 by X%\n  → call OUR contract (liquidate / borrow) — it reads the moved slot0\n  → swap back, restoring slot0\n  → repay flash loan\n```\n\nThere is no point between step 2 and step 4 at which any other actor can execute. Arbitrage\nrestores the *pool* after the transaction lands; it does not restore *our money*. Same-block\narbitrage is a defence against manipulation that has to *persist* (a TWAP). It is no defence at\nall against manipulation that only has to exist for one `SLOAD`.\n\n**2. \"They would push tens of millions through it and eat the loss.\"**\n\nThey don't eat the notional, they eat the *round trip*. Push in and pull back out of a\nconstant-function AMM with nothing in between, and you end up where you started minus fees on\nboth legs. On a 0.05% pool that is ~0.10% of notional. Flash loans supply the capital\n(Balancer / Morpho / Uniswap flash = 0 fee; Aave v3 = 0.05%), so no capital is at risk overnight\nand none of it needs to be the attacker's.\n\n**3. \"Our own on-chain reserve of truth.\"**\n\n`slot0` is not a reserve of truth. It is the instantaneous tick, i.e. *the exact value the last\nswap in the pool wrote*. It is an attacker-writable storage slot with a published price list.\nAlso note \"$200M of liquidity\" is TVL, not depth: V3 liquidity is concentrated, typically within\n~±1% of spot on this pair, and thins sharply outside that band. TVL tells you almost nothing\nabout the cost of a 10% excursion.\n\nThe stated objection to Chainlink — \"it puts a third party between us and our liquidations\" — is\nreal but inverted. `slot0` puts *any anonymous flash-loan borrower* between us and our\nliquidations. We are not choosing between trust and no-trust; we are choosing which party we\ntrust. Aave, Compound and Spark price the same pair off the same Chainlink feed with billions\noutstanding.\n\n---\n\n## Cost side: what a 10% read actually costs\n\n### The notional\n\nFor a V3 pool with active liquidity `L` at price `P` (USDC per WETH):\n\n```\npush price UP   to 1.1P:  USDC in ≈ L·√P · (√1.1 − 1)  = 0.0488 · L√P\npush price DOWN to 0.9P:  WETH in ≈ (L/√P) · (1/√0.9 − 1) = 0.0541 · L/√P\n```\n\n`L√P` is the virtual USDC reserve. Anchoring it from observed depth (a $Q trade moving price by\na small ε implies `L√P ≈ 2Q/ε`), and taking $1M → ~15bps as a working figure for this pool,\ngives `L√P ≈ $1.3B` and a uniform-liquidity estimate of ~$65M for a 10% move.\n\nThat is an **upper bound**, and deliberately so: it assumes `L` stays constant across the whole\n10% range, when in reality it collapses once you leave the concentrated band. The true number is\nlower — call it **$20M–$100M of notional**.\n\n**This range does not matter to the conclusion**, which is the important point:\n\n### The cost\n\n| Component | Basis | At $30M notional | At $100M notional |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Pool fee, leg 1 | 0.05% of in | $15k | $50k |\n| Pool fee, leg 2 (unwind) | 0.05% of in | $15k | $50k |\n| Flash loan | 0% (Balancer/Morpho/UniV3) – 0.05% (Aave) | $0 – $15k | $0 – $50k |\n| Gas | ~1–2M gas | < $1k | < $1k |\n| Builder tip / bundle inclusion | discretionary | $5k – $50k | $5k – $50k |\n| **Total** | **≈ 0.1% of notional + tip** | **~$35k–$80k** | **~$105k–$200k** |\n\nCost scales with **0.1% of notional**, so even if my depth estimate is off by 3×, the attack\nstill costs low six figures. The $200M TVL figure is doing no work in the attacker's budget,\nbecause they rent the capital for one transaction and pay only the fee.\n\n### And 10% is generous to us\n\nThe attacker does not need 10%. Borrower LTVs cluster just under the threshold, so a smaller\nmove catches whatever is closest to the line, at proportionally lower cost:\n\n| Down-move | Positions it makes liquidatable | Attacker's margin per $ repaid (8% bonus) |\n|---|---|---|\n| 4% | true LTV ≥ 81.6% | 12.5% |\n| 7% | true LTV ≥ 79.1% | 16.1% |\n| 10% | true LTV ≥ 76.5% | 20.0% |\n\n(Liquidatable when `trueLTV / (1−m) ≥ 0.85`, so threshold = `0.85 · (1−m)`.\nMargin = `(1+bonus)/(1−m) − 1`.)\n\nA 4% move needs roughly 40% of the notional of a 10% move, so ~$15k–$30k all-in.\n\n---\n\n## Payoff side: what they get\n\n### Attack A — push the price DOWN, liquidate healthy borrowers (this is the live one)\n\nWorked example, one $2M position at 80% true LTV:\n\n```\nCollateral   $2.0M WETH,  debt $1.6M USDC,  true LTV 80%  → healthy\nManipulate  −10%:  collateral reads $1.8M   → LTV 88.9%   → liquidatable\nLiquidator repays 50% close factor          = $800k USDC\nReceives    $800k × 1.08 (bonus) at the manipulated price\n            = $864k of \"value\" = $864k / 0.9 = $960k of WETH at true market price\nProfit      $960k − $800k = $160k on one position\n```\n\nThat is **20% of the repaid amount**, versus a ~$35k–$80k attack cost. And the transaction is\natomic, so the attacker sweeps *every* qualifying position in the same call — the $2M per-position\ncap does not bound the attack, it only bounds one row of it. The bonus paid out here is not\nprotocol-neutral: it is value taken directly out of solvent borrowers who were never actually\nundercollateralised.\n\n**Break-even.** Profitable when\n\n```\n0.20 · R  >  0.001 · N + tip\n```\n\nwith `R` = collateral repaid, `N` = manipulation notional. At `N = $60M`, tip $50k:\n`R > ~$550k`. We need under a million dollars of borrowers sitting above 76.5% LTV in a single\nblock for this to pay. At any meaningful book size that condition is permanently satisfied.\n\n### Attack B — push the price UP, over-borrow, walk away (not viable at 10%)\n\nDeposit $2M of real WETH, manipulate +10% so it reads $2.2M, borrow 85% = $1.87M, abandon.\nNet: **−$130k**. The position is still genuinely over-collateralised, liquidators clean it up,\nand the attacker eats the bonus. Break-even needs `0.85 · (1+m) > 1`, i.e. an **~17.6% up-move**,\nwhich is materially more expensive.\n\nSame arithmetic kills the self-liquidation variant of Attack A: the bonus comes out of the\nattacker's own collateral, so it's a wash unless the move is deep enough to leave bad debt\n(again ~17.6%+).\n\n**So the vector we are actually exposed to at 10% is A: liquidating other people's healthy\npositions.** It is the cheaper attack *and* the more profitable one.\n\n### Attack C — no attacker at all\n\n`slot0` at the top of a block reflects the *end of the previous block*. During a fast market\nmove it is systematically stale by up to 12 seconds, and a searcher winning top-of-block gets a\n1–3% error for free, with zero attack cost and nothing to detect. Ordinary large swaps and\nsandwich bundles produce the same transient error. This alone disqualifies `slot0` for\nliquidations even in a world with no adversary.\n\n---\n\n## What we should price with\n\n**Primary: Chainlink push feeds, ETH/USD ÷ USDC/USD.**\n\nPrice the debt too — do not assume USDC = $1. A depeg with hardcoded $1 debt understates LTV\nexactly when we most need it accurate.\n\n```\npriceEthInUsdc = ethUsd * 1e(usdcUsdDecimals) / usdcUsd   // scale explicitly, read decimals\n```\n\nMainnet feed parameters to confirm on-chain before shipping (these do change):\nETH/USD ≈ 0.5% deviation threshold / 1h heartbeat; USDC/USD ≈ 0.25% / 24h.\n\n**Secondary: a 30–60 minute Uniswap V3 TWAP via `observe()`, used as a tripwire, not a price.**\n\nA TWAP has a completely different cost model from `slot0` — the attacker must *hold* the price\nagainst arbitrageurs for the whole window, with real capital at risk across many blocks and no\natomicity, which is orders of magnitude more expensive. It is still not good enough to be our\nprimary (JIT liquidity withdrawal and multi-block MEV, where a proposer controls consecutive\nslots, both cut that cost materially), but it is a fine independent check. To break us, an\nattacker then has to corrupt both sources at once.\n\nIf we use it: read `slot0.observationCardinality` and call `increaseObservationCardinalityNext`\nso the pool actually retains enough observations to cover our window. A pool that hasn't been\ngrown will silently give you a much shorter TWAP than you asked for.\n\n---\n\n## Checks required around the price, before it touches a health calculation\n\n1. **`latestRoundData()`, never `latestAnswer()`.** The latter has no timestamp — you cannot\n   detect staleness at all.\n2. **`answer > 0`** — revert on zero or negative. A zero price makes every position instantly\n   liquidatable.\n3. **Staleness: `block.timestamp - updatedAt <= maxStaleness`**, configured **per feed** from\n   that feed's heartbeat plus a buffer (e.g. heartbeat + 25%). A single global constant is wrong\n   here: ETH/USD is 1h and USDC/USD is 24h, and a threshold that works for one is broken for the\n   other in one direction or the other.\n4. **Aggregator `minAnswer` / `maxAnswer` bounds.** Some feeds still clamp the reported answer at\n   a floor. This is the Venus/LUNA failure mode: the real price crashed, the feed reported the\n   floor, and the protocol happily lent against a worthless asset. Check the answer is strictly\n   inside the aggregator's bounds, or keep our own absolute sanity band. Newer feeds have\n   removed these — check the specific aggregator we deploy against.\n5. **Read `decimals()` from the feed**, don't hardcode 8. And normalise scale in one shared\n   library so collateral and debt cannot drift apart.\n6. **Divergence guard.** Compare Chainlink against the TWAP; if `|Δ| > 2–5%`, treat the price as\n   untrusted and enter the degraded mode below rather than picking one.\n7. **Same price on both sides of the health check.** Never value collateral from one source and\n   debt from another within a single evaluation — that differential is its own exploit. Take\n   conservatism through the LTV parameter, not through mixing oracles.\n8. **Sequencer uptime feed** — not applicable on mainnet, but required the moment we deploy to\n   an L2. Worth putting the hook in now.\n\n### Failure policy (decide this explicitly, it's the part that usually gets skipped)\n\nDo **not** fall back to a DEX spot price when Chainlink is stale — that is a strictly worse\noracle reachable by simply waiting, which converts an availability problem into a solvency\nproblem.\n\nAsymmetric degraded mode:\n\n- **Halt new borrows and new withdrawals immediately** on stale/invalid/divergent price. Fail\n  closed on anything that increases risk.\n- **Do not blanket-halt liquidations.** Freezing liquidations during a crash is itself a\n  solvency risk — bad debt accrues while we're paused. Instead, allow liquidations to continue\n  against a second independent source (a second provider such as Redstone or Pyth, or the long\n  TWAP), and only under the divergence guard.\n- **Per-block liquidation cap** — a circuit breaker on how much collateral can be seized in one\n  block. This bounds the damage from *any* successful oracle attack, including one against a\n  source we currently trust, and costs almost nothing in normal operation.\n\n### Parameter note: 85% is aggressive for this stack\n\nThe 15% buffer between the liquidation threshold and insolvency has to absorb, simultaneously:\noracle deviation band (~0.5%), heartbeat lag during a fast move (which on a violent ETH day is\nthe big one), the liquidation bonus (5–10%), and gas/slippage for the liquidator. That is most\nof 15% before ETH has moved. 80–82.5% is the defensible number for WETH/USDC on a 1h heartbeat\nfeed; if we keep 85%, it should be a deliberate, written-down decision rather than an inherited\ndefault.\n\n---\n\n## To verify before this is final\n\n- Measure actual pool depth rather than trusting my estimate: pull the tick/liquidity\n  distribution for the WETH/USDC 5bp pool and simulate the swap size for −4%, −7% and −10%.\n  Also check the real *cost* is the ~0.1% round trip I've assumed. I expect this to make the\n  attack look cheaper than the numbers above, not more expensive.\n- Confirm current live deviation threshold, heartbeat, decimals and min/max bounds for both\n  feeds on-chain, not from docs.\n- Query our own book: how much collateral currently sits above 76.5% LTV? That number is the\n  attacker's payday and it should go on a dashboard.\n- Alerting: Chainlink-vs-TWAP divergence, and staleness approaching the limit — both should page\n  before the contract reverts, not after.\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":578,"cache_read_input_tokens":32051,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":578},"output_tokens":3,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"78730e93-69a2-4a15-be93-c5aa1e1719e5","uuid":"0f9f1bd0-1ca1-4393-ab4c-18d18087c632","timestamp":"2026-07-28T12:23:15.032Z","request_id":"req_011CdUStQitBd6vCAfV4ovnG"}
{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01BkAJBkZehMnGxW6fY7qC6R","type":"tool_result","content":"File created successfully at: /Users/liana/Documents/prog/buidl-guidl/ethskills-evals/artifacts/security-quiz-002/2026-07-28T121924Z-claude-no-skill-1/workspace/answer.md (file state is current in your context — no need to Read it back)"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"78730e93-69a2-4a15-be93-c5aa1e1719e5","uuid":"6efac2ae-3464-4082-a043-16b2bfbe1a4b","timestamp":"2026-07-28T12:23:15.050Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"create","filePath":"/Users/liana/Documents/prog/buidl-guidl/ethskills-evals/artifacts/security-quiz-002/2026-07-28T121924Z-claude-no-skill-1/workspace/answer.md","content":"# Collateral pricing review — Uniswap V3 `slot0` vs. Chainlink\n\n## Bottom line\n\nThe proposal is not \"strictly better,\" it is exploitable for roughly the cost of a swap fee.\nMoving `slot0` 10% at the moment we read it costs an attacker on the order of **$30k–$200k**,\nnot \"tens of millions.\" The tens of millions is *notional flow*, and the attacker returns it in\nthe same transaction. What they get back is **~20% of everything they can liquidate in that\nblock**, which breaks even at around **$0.5M–$1M of borrower positions**. We should be pricing\ncollateral off Chainlink ETH/USD and USDC/USD, with the pool used only as a divergence tripwire.\n\n---\n\n## Where the argument breaks\n\nThree load-bearing claims are wrong.\n\n**1. \"Arbitrage bots would drag it back within the same block.\"**\n\nThey cannot. The attack is a single atomic transaction:\n\n```\nflash-borrow USDC/WETH\n  → swap into the pool, moving slot0 by X%\n  → call OUR contract (liquidate / borrow) — it reads the moved slot0\n  → swap back, restoring slot0\n  → repay flash loan\n```\n\nThere is no point between step 2 and step 4 at which any other actor can execute. Arbitrage\nrestores the *pool* after the transaction lands; it does not restore *our money*. Same-block\narbitrage is a defence against manipulation that has to *persist* (a TWAP). It is no defence at\nall against manipulation that only has to exist for one `SLOAD`.\n\n**2. \"They would push tens of millions through it and eat the loss.\"**\n\nThey don't eat the notional, they eat the *round trip*. Push in and pull back out of a\nconstant-function AMM with nothing in between, and you end up where you started minus fees on\nboth legs. On a 0.05% pool that is ~0.10% of notional. Flash loans supply the capital\n(Balancer / Morpho / Uniswap flash = 0 fee; Aave v3 = 0.05%), so no capital is at risk overnight\nand none of it needs to be the attacker's.\n\n**3. \"Our own on-chain reserve of truth.\"**\n\n`slot0` is not a reserve of truth. It is the instantaneous tick, i.e. *the exact value the last\nswap in the pool wrote*. It is an attacker-writable storage slot with a published price list.\nAlso note \"$200M of liquidity\" is TVL, not depth: V3 liquidity is concentrated, typically within\n~±1% of spot on this pair, and thins sharply outside that band. TVL tells you almost nothing\nabout the cost of a 10% excursion.\n\nThe stated objection to Chainlink — \"it puts a third party between us and our liquidations\" — is\nreal but inverted. `slot0` puts *any anonymous flash-loan borrower* between us and our\nliquidations. We are not choosing between trust and no-trust; we are choosing which party we\ntrust. Aave, Compound and Spark price the same pair off the same Chainlink feed with billions\noutstanding.\n\n---\n\n## Cost side: what a 10% read actually costs\n\n### The notional\n\nFor a V3 pool with active liquidity `L` at price `P` (USDC per WETH):\n\n```\npush price UP   to 1.1P:  USDC in ≈ L·√P · (√1.1 − 1)  = 0.0488 · L√P\npush price DOWN to 0.9P:  WETH in ≈ (L/√P) · (1/√0.9 − 1) = 0.0541 · L/√P\n```\n\n`L√P` is the virtual USDC reserve. Anchoring it from observed depth (a $Q trade moving price by\na small ε implies `L√P ≈ 2Q/ε`), and taking $1M → ~15bps as a working figure for this pool,\ngives `L√P ≈ $1.3B` and a uniform-liquidity estimate of ~$65M for a 10% move.\n\nThat is an **upper bound**, and deliberately so: it assumes `L` stays constant across the whole\n10% range, when in reality it collapses once you leave the concentrated band. The true number is\nlower — call it **$20M–$100M of notional**.\n\n**This range does not matter to the conclusion**, which is the important point:\n\n### The cost\n\n| Component | Basis | At $30M notional | At $100M notional |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Pool fee, leg 1 | 0.05% of in | $15k | $50k |\n| Pool fee, leg 2 (unwind) | 0.05% of in | $15k | $50k |\n| Flash loan | 0% (Balancer/Morpho/UniV3) – 0.05% (Aave) | $0 – $15k | $0 – $50k |\n| Gas | ~1–2M gas | < $1k | < $1k |\n| Builder tip / bundle inclusion | discretionary | $5k – $50k | $5k – $50k |\n| **Total** | **≈ 0.1% of notional + tip** | **~$35k–$80k** | **~$105k–$200k** |\n\nCost scales with **0.1% of notional**, so even if my depth estimate is off by 3×, the attack\nstill costs low six figures. The $200M TVL figure is doing no work in the attacker's budget,\nbecause they rent the capital for one transaction and pay only the fee.\n\n### And 10% is generous to us\n\nThe attacker does not need 10%. Borrower LTVs cluster just under the threshold, so a smaller\nmove catches whatever is closest to the line, at proportionally lower cost:\n\n| Down-move | Positions it makes liquidatable | Attacker's margin per $ repaid (8% bonus) |\n|---|---|---|\n| 4% | true LTV ≥ 81.6% | 12.5% |\n| 7% | true LTV ≥ 79.1% | 16.1% |\n| 10% | true LTV ≥ 76.5% | 20.0% |\n\n(Liquidatable when `trueLTV / (1−m) ≥ 0.85`, so threshold = `0.85 · (1−m)`.\nMargin = `(1+bonus)/(1−m) − 1`.)\n\nA 4% move needs roughly 40% of the notional of a 10% move, so ~$15k–$30k all-in.\n\n---\n\n## Payoff side: what they get\n\n### Attack A — push the price DOWN, liquidate healthy borrowers (this is the live one)\n\nWorked example, one $2M position at 80% true LTV:\n\n```\nCollateral   $2.0M WETH,  debt $1.6M USDC,  true LTV 80%  → healthy\nManipulate  −10%:  collateral reads $1.8M   → LTV 88.9%   → liquidatable\nLiquidator repays 50% close factor          = $800k USDC\nReceives    $800k × 1.08 (bonus) at the manipulated price\n            = $864k of \"value\" = $864k / 0.9 = $960k of WETH at true market price\nProfit      $960k − $800k = $160k on one position\n```\n\nThat is **20% of the repaid amount**, versus a ~$35k–$80k attack cost. And the transaction is\natomic, so the attacker sweeps *every* qualifying position in the same call — the $2M per-position\ncap does not bound the attack, it only bounds one row of it. The bonus paid out here is not\nprotocol-neutral: it is value taken directly out of solvent borrowers who were never actually\nundercollateralised.\n\n**Break-even.** Profitable when\n\n```\n0.20 · R  >  0.001 · N + tip\n```\n\nwith `R` = collateral repaid, `N` = manipulation notional. At `N = $60M`, tip $50k:\n`R > ~$550k`. We need under a million dollars of borrowers sitting above 76.5% LTV in a single\nblock for this to pay. At any meaningful book size that condition is permanently satisfied.\n\n### Attack B — push the price UP, over-borrow, walk away (not viable at 10%)\n\nDeposit $2M of real WETH, manipulate +10% so it reads $2.2M, borrow 85% = $1.87M, abandon.\nNet: **−$130k**. The position is still genuinely over-collateralised, liquidators clean it up,\nand the attacker eats the bonus. Break-even needs `0.85 · (1+m) > 1`, i.e. an **~17.6% up-move**,\nwhich is materially more expensive.\n\nSame arithmetic kills the self-liquidation variant of Attack A: the bonus comes out of the\nattacker's own collateral, so it's a wash unless the move is deep enough to leave bad debt\n(again ~17.6%+).\n\n**So the vector we are actually exposed to at 10% is A: liquidating other people's healthy\npositions.** It is the cheaper attack *and* the more profitable one.\n\n### Attack C — no attacker at all\n\n`slot0` at the top of a block reflects the *end of the previous block*. During a fast market\nmove it is systematically stale by up to 12 seconds, and a searcher winning top-of-block gets a\n1–3% error for free, with zero attack cost and nothing to detect. Ordinary large swaps and\nsandwich bundles produce the same transient error. This alone disqualifies `slot0` for\nliquidations even in a world with no adversary.\n\n---\n\n## What we should price with\n\n**Primary: Chainlink push feeds, ETH/USD ÷ USDC/USD.**\n\nPrice the debt too — do not assume USDC = $1. A depeg with hardcoded $1 debt understates LTV\nexactly when we most need it accurate.\n\n```\npriceEthInUsdc = ethUsd * 1e(usdcUsdDecimals) / usdcUsd   // scale explicitly, read decimals\n```\n\nMainnet feed parameters to confirm on-chain before shipping (these do change):\nETH/USD ≈ 0.5% deviation threshold / 1h heartbeat; USDC/USD ≈ 0.25% / 24h.\n\n**Secondary: a 30–60 minute Uniswap V3 TWAP via `observe()`, used as a tripwire, not a price.**\n\nA TWAP has a completely different cost model from `slot0` — the attacker must *hold* the price\nagainst arbitrageurs for the whole window, with real capital at risk across many blocks and no\natomicity, which is orders of magnitude more expensive. It is still not good enough to be our\nprimary (JIT liquidity withdrawal and multi-block MEV, where a proposer controls consecutive\nslots, both cut that cost materially), but it is a fine independent check. To break us, an\nattacker then has to corrupt both sources at once.\n\nIf we use it: read `slot0.observationCardinality` and call `increaseObservationCardinalityNext`\nso the pool actually retains enough observations to cover our window. A pool that hasn't been\ngrown will silently give you a much shorter TWAP than you asked for.\n\n---\n\n## Checks required around the price, before it touches a health calculation\n\n1. **`latestRoundData()`, never `latestAnswer()`.** The latter has no timestamp — you cannot\n   detect staleness at all.\n2. **`answer > 0`** — revert on zero or negative. A zero price makes every position instantly\n   liquidatable.\n3. **Staleness: `block.timestamp - updatedAt <= maxStaleness`**, configured **per feed** from\n   that feed's heartbeat plus a buffer (e.g. heartbeat + 25%). A single global constant is wrong\n   here: ETH/USD is 1h and USDC/USD is 24h, and a threshold that works for one is broken for the\n   other in one direction or the other.\n4. **Aggregator `minAnswer` / `maxAnswer` bounds.** Some feeds still clamp the reported answer at\n   a floor. This is the Venus/LUNA failure mode: the real price crashed, the feed reported the\n   floor, and the protocol happily lent against a worthless asset. Check the answer is strictly\n   inside the aggregator's bounds, or keep our own absolute sanity band. Newer feeds have\n   removed these — check the specific aggregator we deploy against.\n5. **Read `decimals()` from the feed**, don't hardcode 8. And normalise scale in one shared\n   library so collateral and debt cannot drift apart.\n6. **Divergence guard.** Compare Chainlink against the TWAP; if `|Δ| > 2–5%`, treat the price as\n   untrusted and enter the degraded mode below rather than picking one.\n7. **Same price on both sides of the health check.** Never value collateral from one source and\n   debt from another within a single evaluation — that differential is its own exploit. Take\n   conservatism through the LTV parameter, not through mixing oracles.\n8. **Sequencer uptime feed** — not applicable on mainnet, but required the moment we deploy to\n   an L2. Worth putting the hook in now.\n\n### Failure policy (decide this explicitly, it's the part that usually gets skipped)\n\nDo **not** fall back to a DEX spot price when Chainlink is stale — that is a strictly worse\noracle reachable by simply waiting, which converts an availability problem into a solvency\nproblem.\n\nAsymmetric degraded mode:\n\n- **Halt new borrows and new withdrawals immediately** on stale/invalid/divergent price. Fail\n  closed on anything that increases risk.\n- **Do not blanket-halt liquidations.** Freezing liquidations during a crash is itself a\n  solvency risk — bad debt accrues while we're paused. Instead, allow liquidations to continue\n  against a second independent source (a second provider such as Redstone or Pyth, or the long\n  TWAP), and only under the divergence guard.\n- **Per-block liquidation cap** — a circuit breaker on how much collateral can be seized in one\n  block. This bounds the damage from *any* successful oracle attack, including one against a\n  source we currently trust, and costs almost nothing in normal operation.\n\n### Parameter note: 85% is aggressive for this stack\n\nThe 15% buffer between the liquidation threshold and insolvency has to absorb, simultaneously:\noracle deviation band (~0.5%), heartbeat lag during a fast move (which on a violent ETH day is\nthe big one), the liquidation bonus (5–10%), and gas/slippage for the liquidator. That is most\nof 15% before ETH has moved. 80–82.5% is the defensible number for WETH/USDC on a 1h heartbeat\nfeed; if we keep 85%, it should be a deliberate, written-down decision rather than an inherited\ndefault.\n\n---\n\n## To verify before this is final\n\n- Measure actual pool depth rather than trusting my estimate: pull the tick/liquidity\n  distribution for the WETH/USDC 5bp pool and simulate the swap size for −4%, −7% and −10%.\n  Also check the real *cost* is the ~0.1% round trip I've assumed. I expect this to make the\n  attack look cheaper than the numbers above, not more expensive.\n- Confirm current live deviation threshold, heartbeat, decimals and min/max bounds for both\n  feeds on-chain, not from docs.\n- Query our own book: how much collateral currently sits above 76.5% LTV? That number is the\n  attacker's payday and it should go on a dashboard.\n- Alerting: Chainlink-vs-TWAP divergence, and staleness approaching the limit — both should page\n  before the contract reverts, not after.\n","structuredPatch":[],"originalFile":null,"userModified":false}}
